::: {.callout-note title="Analogy: a library's request desk"}
A big library won't let you wander the archives. It has a **request desk** with a printed list of what you may ask for and how ("Form B: list all books on a shelf; write the shelf number here"). That list is the **API documentation**. The desk hands results back in a standard format, a few pages at a time ("page 1 of 4: ask again for page 2"), and limits how many requests one visitor may make per hour. Show a library card (a **token**) and the limit goes up.
:::

## What a web API is

An **API** (Application Programming Interface) is a way for programs to use another system's features. A **web API** does it over HTTP (lesson 2.3): you send requests to documented URLs and get structured data back, almost always as JSON (lesson 1.9).

A **REST** API organises those URLs around **resources** (things) and uses HTTP methods as the verbs:

| Request | Means |
|---|---|
| `GET /repos/pytorch/ignite` | read the repository |
| `GET /repos/pytorch/ignite/issues` | list its issues |
| `GET /repos/pytorch/ignite/issues/3932` | read one issue |
| `GET /repos/pytorch/ignite/commits` | list its commits |

GitHub documents every endpoint in its REST API reference at docs.github.com, including parameters, response fields and limits. Reading API documentation is a core backend skill: in the job, you'll integrate with payment providers, email services and AI model APIs the same way.

## httpx

`httpx` is a popular Python library for HTTP. Add it to `my-atlas` as a **runtime** dependency (lesson 1.10):

```bash
uv add httpx
```

A first real call, to this course's own public repository:

```python
import httpx

headers = {"Accept": "application/vnd.github+json", "User-Agent": "atlas-course"}
with httpx.Client(base_url="https://api.github.com", headers=headers, timeout=10.0) as client:
    response = client.get(
        "/repos/ashu-tagore/Learning_FastAPI/issues",
        params={"state": "all", "per_page": 2},
    )
    print(response.status_code, response.headers["content-type"])
    print(response.url)
    items = response.json()
    print(type(items), len(items))
    first = items[0]
    print(first["number"], first["state"], "pull_request" in first)
    print(response.links["next"]["url"][:80], "...")
    print("remaining requests:", response.headers["x-ratelimit-remaining"])

    missing = client.get("/repos/ashu-tagore/Learning_FastAPI/issues/99999")
    print(missing.status_code, missing.json()["message"])
```
```text
200 application/json; charset=utf-8
https://api.github.com/repos/ashu-tagore/Learning_FastAPI/issues?state=all&per_page=2
<class 'list'> 2
3 closed True
https://api.github.com/repositories/1299106774/issues?state=all&per_page=2&after ...
remaining requests: 14982
404 Not Found
```

(The remaining count is high because this was captured on an authenticated network; see rate limits below.)

What's happening:

- `httpx.Client` keeps connections open and reuses them across requests (skipping repeated TCP and TLS handshakes, lessons 2.2 and 2.3), and applies `base_url`, `headers` and `timeout` to every request. Use it in a `with` block so connections are closed.
- `params` builds the query string for you, escaping spaces and special characters. You never paste `?state=all&...` together by hand.
- `response.json()` parses the JSON body into Python lists and dicts.
- **Always set a timeout.** Without one, a stuck server can hang your program forever.
- Look at `"pull_request" in first`: this "issue" #3 is really a pull request. GitHub's issues endpoint returns **both**, and marks pull requests with a `pull_request` key. Atlas must skip them.
- A 404 is still a valid HTTP response. httpx doesn't raise an exception for it; checking the status is your job.

## Pagination

APIs return long lists in **pages**. GitHub returns up to 30 items per request by default (100 with `per_page=100`) and tells you where the next page is in the `Link` header (lesson 2.3). httpx parses it into `response.links`. When there's no `next` link, you're on the last page.

```{mermaid}
sequenceDiagram
  participant A as Atlas
  participant G as GitHub API
  A->>G: GET /repos/pytorch/ignite/issues?labels=good first issue&per_page=100
  G-->>A: 100 items + a Link header pointing to page 2
  A->>G: GET (the "next" URL)
  G-->>A: 37 items, no "next" link
  Note over A: done: 137 items
```

Always follow the link GitHub gives you rather than building page URLs yourself: as the output above shows, GitHub's next-page URL can include a cursor (`after=...`) you couldn't have guessed.

## Authentication and rate limits

Public data needs no login, but anonymous clients get **60 requests per hour**, shared by everyone at your IP address. With a **personal access token** the limit is 5,000 per hour. Every response tells you where you stand:

| Header | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `x-ratelimit-limit` | requests allowed per hour |
| `x-ratelimit-remaining` | requests left |
| `x-ratelimit-reset` | when the count resets, as a Unix timestamp (seconds since 1 January 1970, UTC) |

When you run out, GitHub answers `403` or `429` with `x-ratelimit-remaining: 0`.

To get a token: on GitHub, **Settings → Developer settings → Personal access tokens → Fine-grained tokens → Generate new token**. Give it an expiry date and **public repositories, read-only** access. Atlas needs nothing more, and a token that can't write can't do damage if it leaks.

Give it to your program through an **environment variable** (lesson 0.2), never in the code:

```bash
export GITHUB_TOKEN=github_pat_...
```

```python
import os

token = os.environ.get("GITHUB_TOKEN")  # None if not set
```

It travels in the `Authorization: Bearer <token>` header, only ever over HTTPS. Never print it, log it or commit it. (In Part 4, settings move into a proper configuration object instead of reading `os.environ` directly.)

## In the project: `github.py`

Create `src/atlas/github.py`:

```python
"""Read-only access to the GitHub REST API.

Atlas never writes to GitHub, so this module only ever sends GET requests.
"""

from dataclasses import dataclass
from datetime import datetime
from typing import Any

import httpx

GITHUB_API = "https://api.github.com"


class GitHubError(Exception):
    """A problem talking to GitHub, explained in words a user can act on."""


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Issue:
    number: int
    title: str
    url: str
    author: str
    labels: tuple[str, ...]
    comments: int
    created_at: datetime


def build_headers(token: str | None) -> dict[str, str]:
    headers = {
        "Accept": "application/vnd.github+json",
        "X-GitHub-Api-Version": "2022-11-28",
        # GitHub rejects requests without a User-Agent.
        "User-Agent": "atlas-course",
    }
    if token:
        headers["Authorization"] = f"Bearer {token}"
    return headers


def check_response(response: httpx.Response) -> None:
    """Raise GitHubError with a clear message unless the response succeeded."""
    if response.is_success:
        return
    out_of_requests = response.headers.get("x-ratelimit-remaining") == "0"
    if out_of_requests:
        raise GitHubError("GitHub rate limit reached; try again later or set GITHUB_TOKEN")
    if response.status_code == 404:
        raise GitHubError(f"not found on GitHub: {response.request.url.path}")
    raise GitHubError(f"GitHub answered {response.status_code}: {response.text[:200]}")


def parse_issue(item: dict[str, Any]) -> Issue:
    return Issue(
        number=item["number"],
        title=item["title"],
        url=item["html_url"],
        author=item["user"]["login"],
        labels=tuple(label["name"] for label in item["labels"]),
        comments=item["comments"],
        created_at=datetime.fromisoformat(item["created_at"]),
    )


def fetch_issues(
    repo: str,
    label: str,
    *,
    token: str | None = None,
    max_pages: int = 10,
    transport: httpx.BaseTransport | None = None,
) -> list[Issue]:
    """All open issues in repo carrying the label, following pagination."""
    url = f"/repos/{repo}/issues"
    params: dict[str, str | int] | None = {"state": "open", "labels": label, "per_page": 100}
    issues: list[Issue] = []

    with httpx.Client(
        base_url=GITHUB_API, headers=build_headers(token), timeout=10.0, transport=transport
    ) as client:
        for _ in range(max_pages):
            response = client.get(url, params=params)
            check_response(response)

            for item in response.json():
                # The issues endpoint also returns pull requests; they carry this key.
                is_pull_request = "pull_request" in item
                if is_pull_request:
                    continue
                issues.append(parse_issue(item))

            next_page = response.links.get("next")
            if next_page is None:
                break
            # The "next" link already contains every query parameter.
            url = next_page["url"]
            params = None

    return issues
```

Design choices worth noticing:

- **Raw JSON stops at the border.** `parse_issue` turns GitHub's large, loosely-typed dict (`dict[str, Any]`: "keys are strings, values could be anything") into a small, typed `Issue`. The rest of Atlas never touches GitHub's raw format, so if GitHub changes a field, only `parse_issue` changes.
- **One kind of error.** Every way talking to GitHub can fail becomes a `GitHubError` with a message a human can act on. A custom exception is just a class that inherits from `Exception`: one of the rare places where inheritance is exactly right.
- **`max_pages`** stops a runaway loop if something unexpected keeps returning `next` links.
- **`transport`** lets tests swap the network for a fake GitHub (lesson 2.6). Normal callers never pass it.

Try it from the REPL (`uv run python`) against Ignite:

```python
>>> from atlas.github import fetch_issues
>>> issues = fetch_issues("pytorch/ignite", "good first issue")
>>> len(issues)
>>> issues[0].title
```

You'll see however many good first issues Ignite has open today, as real `Issue` objects.

## Common mistakes

- **No timeout.** Your program can hang forever on a stuck server.
- **Ignoring status codes** and calling `.json()` on an error page, then crashing with a confusing `KeyError`.
- **Treating the issues list as issues only.** Pull requests are included; skip them.
- **Building page URLs by hand** instead of following `Link`.
- **Putting a token in code or a URL.** Use an environment variable and the `Authorization` header.
- **Burning the rate limit while developing** by re-fetching on every run. The next lesson adds a cache.

## Check yourself

**1.** Why does Atlas convert GitHub's JSON into `Issue` objects right away?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Answer"}
So the rest of the code works with a small, typed, documented structure instead of GitHub's raw format. If GitHub's format changes, only `parse_issue` needs to change, and mypy can check every use of `Issue`.
:::

**2.** How does Atlas know it has reached the last page?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Answer"}
The response has no `next` entry in its `Link` header, so `response.links.get("next")` returns `None`.
:::

**3.** What permissions should Atlas's GitHub token have, and why?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Read-only access to public repositories, with an expiry date. Atlas only reads, and a token that can't write is harmless if it leaks.
:::

## Exercise

Write `fetch_repository(repo, token=None) -> dict[str, Any]` that returns a dict with just `full_name`, `stars` (`stargazers_count`), `open_issues` (`open_issues_count`) and `default_branch`, using `GET /repos/{repo}` and `check_response`. Print it for `pytorch/ignite`.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Solution"}
```python
def fetch_repository(repo: str, *, token: str | None = None) -> dict[str, Any]:
    with httpx.Client(base_url=GITHUB_API, headers=build_headers(token), timeout=10.0) as client:
        response = client.get(f"/repos/{repo}")
    check_response(response)
    data = response.json()
    return {
        "full_name": data["full_name"],
        "stars": data["stargazers_count"],
        "open_issues": data["open_issues_count"],
        "default_branch": data["default_branch"],
    }
```

Note: GitHub's `open_issues_count` includes open pull requests, for the same historical reason the issues endpoint returns them.
:::

## Stretch

Make `check_response` report *when* the rate limit resets, in a readable form like `resets at 10:42 UTC`, using the `x-ratelimit-reset` header and `datetime.fromtimestamp(seconds, tz=UTC)`.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Solution"}
```python
from datetime import UTC, datetime

    if out_of_requests:
        reset_epoch = int(response.headers.get("x-ratelimit-reset", "0"))
        reset_at = datetime.fromtimestamp(reset_epoch, tz=UTC).strftime("%H:%M UTC")
        raise GitHubError(f"GitHub rate limit reached; it resets at {reset_at}")
```

`UTC` is a shortcut for `timezone.utc`, available since Python 3.11. This is what the reference code does.
:::

`my-atlas` has a `github.py` module that fetches open issues by label, following pagination, with clear errors. Commit: `feat: Fetched issues from the GitHub API`.
